# Clinical Data Standards: CDISC, SDTM, and ADaM {#sec-cdisc}

Alumni of this program who now work for pharmaceutical sponsors
and contract research organizations (CROs) report the same first
week: data structures, variable names, and regulatory conventions
that their statistics courses never mentioned. One of those
conventions produces a wrong answer without an error. The
time-to-event datasets they are handed code an event as `CNSR = 0`
and censoring as a positive number, the reverse of what
`survival::Surv()` expects, so `Surv(AVAL, CNSR)` runs, draws a
plausible curve, and estimates the curve of censoring instead of
the curve of events. This chapter builds the standard datasets for
the running HF-HOME trial, from the tabulation layer a sponsor
submits to the analysis datasets you will specify and check, and
shows where each convention can go silently wrong.

## From protocol to submission {#sec-cdisc-pipeline}

The Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) is a
non-profit that publishes data standards for clinical research.
Since December 2016, the United States Food and Drug
Administration (FDA) has required study data in CDISC formats for
new drug applications (NDAs) and biologics license applications
(BLAs) [@fda2024conformance]. Of the CDISC standards, two are the
statistician's daily material: the Study Data Tabulation Model
(SDTM), the submitted record of what was collected, and the
Analysis Data Model (ADaM), the datasets the analyses run on.[^cdash]

[^cdash]: Two other CDISC standards sit on either side of these.
    CDASH (Clinical Data Acquisition Standards Harmonization)
    standardizes the case report form, so that collected fields
    map cleanly to SDTM; SEND (Standard for Exchange of
    Nonclinical Data) is SDTM's counterpart for animal studies.

### The pipeline and who builds each layer

@fig-cdisc-pipeline shows the flow and the row granularity at each
stage, which is the quantity to track across every join.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-cdisc-pipeline
%%| fig-alt: "Vertical pipeline from protocol and SAP, to the CRF
%%|   for site data entry, to SDTM domains such as DM, EX, AE, LB,
%%|   VS and DS holding one row per observation, to analysis-ready
%%|   ADaM datasets such as ADSL, ADTTE and ADAE, to tables,
%%|   listings and figures, and finally to the CSR and FDA
%%|   submission. Dashed annotations mark SDTM as immutable once
%%|   locked and ADaM as traceable back to SDTM."
%%| fig-cap: "The regulatory data pipeline from protocol to FDA
%%|   submission. SDTM is the immutable source the analysis reads;
%%|   ADaM is the analysis-ready layer derived from it."
flowchart TD
  P["Protocol and SAP<br/><i>design, endpoints, estimands</i>"] --> C["CRF<br/><i>site data entry</i>"]
  C --> S["SDTM domains<br/>DM · EX · AE · LB · VS · DS<br/><i>one row per observation</i>"]
  S --> A["ADaM datasets<br/>ADSL · ADTTE · ADAE<br/><i>analysis-ready</i>"]
  A --> T["TLFs<br/><i>tables, listings, figures</i>"]
  T --> R["CSR and FDA submission<br/><i>Define-XML, aCRF, SDRG, ADRG</i>"]
  S -.->|"immutable once locked"| S
  A -.->|"traceable to SDTM"| S
```

The protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP) define the
trial; sites record observations on case report forms (CRFs); data
management builds the SDTM domains from the collected data; ADaM
datasets are derived from SDTM; and the tables, listings, and
figures (TLFs) of the clinical study report (CSR) are produced
from ADaM. In most sponsors and CROs the work on ADaM is divided.
The biostatistician writes the SAP and, often, the ADaM
specifications; statistical programmers implement the datasets
and the TLFs against those specifications, usually with
independent double programming as validation
(@sec-cdisc-industry). Whichever role you take, your deliverables
will be ADaM specifications, ADaM datasets, or the tables built
from them.

Two rules organize the pipeline. **Immutability**: once SDTM is
locked it is not edited to suit a new analysis; a new analytic
need produces a new ADaM variable. **Traceability**: every ADaM
variable points back to its SDTM source and its derivation,
recorded in the ADaM specification and in Define-XML. The order of
work follows from the second rule: write the specification,
review it, then implement it. Building the dataset first and
writing the specification from the result is a common
antipattern, because the specification is the contract that gets
reviewed.

### The submission package

A submission carries more than datasets. @tbl-cdisc-package lists
the supporting documents a statistician meets; you will rarely
write Define-XML by hand, because tools generate it from the
specification.

| Document | What it is | Typically produced by |
|---|---|---|
| Define-XML | Machine-readable metadata for every variable: type, controlled terminology, derivation, source | Generated from the specifications |
| Annotated CRF (aCRF) | The blank CRF with SDTM variable names on each field | Data management |
| Study Data Reviewer's Guide (SDRG) | Narrative on SDTM conformance and known issues | Data management |
| Analysis Data Reviewer's Guide (ADRG) | Narrative on ADaM datasets and analysis choices | Statistics and programming |
| SAP | Pre-specified analyses, analysis sets, estimands, sensitivity analyses | Biostatistician |

: The documents that accompany SDTM and ADaM in a submission. {#tbl-cdisc-package}

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** SDTM already holds every collected value in a
one-row-per-observation layout, and ADaM adds no new data. Why
build a second layer rather than fit the model on SDTM?

**Answer.** Because ADaM is where the analysis decisions become
explicit, traceable, and reviewable one at a time: which subjects
are in each analysis set, which date starts the clock, how
censoring was assigned, which visit is baseline. Fit the model on
SDTM and those decisions are still made, but inside the modeling
script, mixed together, visible only to whoever reads the code.
The separation is the book's raw and derived data rule
(@sec-acquisition): SDTM is `data/raw/`, ADaM is `data/derived/`.
:::

## SDTM: the data as collected {#sec-cdisc-sdtm}

SDTM organizes a trial's observations into [**domains**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-domain), each a
dataset on one topic. The ones you will meet first are `DM`
(demographics, one row per subject), `EX` (exposure, one row per
dose or dosing interval), `DS` (disposition, one row per
milestone or event), `AE` (adverse events), `LB` (laboratory
results), and `VS` (vital signs). Within a domain each row is a
single observation, and the same variable names (`USUBJID`,
`VISIT`, `--TESTCD`, `--ORRES`, `--STRESN`) recur across domains.
Dates are ISO 8601 character strings such as `'2024-03-15'` or
`'2024-03-15T08:30'`, not `Date` values, because a collected date
can be partial (`'2024-03'`) and a character field holds it as
collected.

### The HF-HOME domains

The HF-HOME generator includes `hfhome_sdtm()`, which builds
minimal `DM`, `EX`, and `DS` domains from the trial: `EX` has one
row per home-health visit, the intervention in this trial, and
`DS` has a `RANDOMIZED` protocol milestone for every subject and
one disposition event (`COMPLETED` at day 30, `DEATH`, or
`LOST TO FOLLOW-UP` for an unascertained outcome). Readmissions
belong in the healthcare-encounters domain, `HO`, which the chunk
builds from the outcome file. Real SDTM has many more variables
per domain; these keep only what the ADaM derivations need.

```{r}
#| label: cdisc-setup
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
library(survival)

source(file.path('..', '..', 'R', 'hfhome.R'))
sdtm <- hfhome_sdtm()
dm <- sdtm$dm
ex <- sdtm$ex
ds <- sdtm$ds

hf_dir <- file.path('..', 'data', 'raw_data', 'hfhome')
read_hf <- function(file) {
  readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, file),
                  col_types = readr::cols(patient_id = 'c',
                                          .default = '?'))
}

ho <- read_hf('outcomes.csv') |>
  filter(!is.na(readmit_date)) |>
  transmute(STUDYID = 'HFHOME', DOMAIN = 'HO',
            USUBJID = paste('HFHOME', patient_id, sep = '-'),
            HOTERM  = 'HOSPITAL READMISSION',
            HOSTDTC = format(readmit_date, '%Y-%m-%d'))

c(DM = nrow(dm), EX = nrow(ex), DS = nrow(ds), HO = nrow(ho))
head(select(dm, USUBJID, SITEID, RFSTDTC, AGE, SEX, ARM, ACTARM), 3)
head(select(ds, USUBJID, DSDECOD, DSCAT, DSSTDTC), 4)
```

`ARM` is the planned arm, as randomized. `ACTARM` is the arm the
subject actually received, here home health if a visit occurred
within 7 days of discharge; the two differ for the nonadherent
patients in both arms.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm the structural promises of each domain before deriving
anything from it: one `DM` row per subject, character dates, two
`DS` rows per subject, and no `EX` or `HO` subject missing from
`DM`.

```{r}
#| label: cdisc-sdtm-verify
stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(dm$USUBJID),
  is.character(dm$RFSTDTC), is.character(ex$EXSTDTC),
  is.character(ds$DSSTDTC), is.character(ho$HOSTDTC),
  all(table(ds$USUBJID) == 2),
  all(ex$USUBJID %in% dm$USUBJID),
  all(ho$USUBJID %in% dm$USUBJID)
)
```

These are structural checks: they confirm the shape the
derivations assume, not that any value is right.
:::

### Controlled terminology

CDISC publishes codelists that enumerate the valid values of
categorical variables. `SEX`, for instance, takes values such as
`'M'`, `'F'`, and `'U'`, not `'Male'`, `'male'`, or `'1'`. The
ADaM specification cites the codelist version for each controlled
variable, and conformance tools reject values outside it.

### Exercises

1. Count the HF-HOME subjects by `ARM` and `ACTARM`, and compute,
   from `DS`, the number of disposition events of each kind by
   planned arm. Which counts would differ if you had grouped by
   `ACTARM`?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-19-1
count(dm, ARM, ACTARM)

ds |>
  filter(DSCAT == 'DISPOSITION EVENT') |>
  left_join(select(dm, USUBJID, ARM), by = 'USUBJID',
            relationship = 'one-to-one') |>
  count(ARM, DSDECOD)
```

Every off-diagonal cell of the first table is a subject whose
received care differs from the assignment. Grouping disposition by
`ACTARM` would move those subjects between arms, so every count in
the second table would change. Analyses as randomized use `ARM`
(in ADaM, `TRT01P`); the treatment actually received belongs to
`ACTARM` (`TRT01A`), which has its own, different uses.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague converts every `--DTC` variable to `Date`
as soon as SDTM is read, 'to save time later'. What is lost?

**Answer.** Partial dates. In a column whose first value is a
complete date, `as.Date()` turns `'2024-03'` into `NA` without an
error, so a collected month and year becomes missing, and the
imputation rule the SAP states for partial dates can no longer be
applied. Keep `--DTC` as character in SDTM and convert in ADaM,
where the conversion and any imputation are part of a documented
derivation (@sec-types).
:::

## ADaM: the data as analyzed {#sec-cdisc-adam}

ADaM datasets take SDTM as input and produce rows and columns
shaped for direct use by statistical procedures. There are three
principal structures, in @tbl-adam-structures; the variables they
share are collected in the ADaM variable card at the end of the
chapter (@tbl-adam-card).

| Structure | Rows | Examples | Key variables |
|---|---|---|---|
| ADSL (subject-level) | Exactly one per subject | `ADSL` | `USUBJID`, `TRT01P`, `TRT01A`, `RANDDT`, population flags |
| BDS (basic data structure) | One per subject, parameter, and analysis timepoint | `ADLB`, `ADVS`, `ADTTE` | `PARAMCD`, `AVAL`, `AVISIT`, `ABLFL`, `BASE`, `CHG`, `CNSR` |
| OCCDS (occurrence data structure) | One per occurrence | `ADAE`, `ADCM` | `AEDECOD`, `ASTDT`, `TRTEMFL` |

: The three ADaM structures. Every other dataset joins back to
`ADSL` by `USUBJID`. {#tbl-adam-structures}

### The censoring convention

In an `ADTTE` dataset, `AVAL` is the time and `CNSR` is the
censoring indicator. HF-HOME will use `1` for a subject followed
to day 30 without an event and `2` for a subject lost to
follow-up.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**`Surv(AVAL, CNSR)` runs and estimates the wrong curve.** CDISC
codes the event as `CNSR = 0` and censoring as a positive integer,
usually `1`, though a sponsor may use `2`, `3`, and so on for
different censoring reasons. `survival::Surv()` expects the
opposite: its second argument is `1` (or `TRUE`) for an event.
Passed unconverted, every censored subject is treated as an event
and every event as censored, so the fitted curve describes
censoring, and the arm with longer follow-up looks worse. The arithmetic
shortcut `Surv(AVAL, 1 - CNSR)` is right only while every censored
row has `CNSR = 1`: a `CNSR = 2` becomes `-1`, which `Surv()`
turns into `NA` with only a warning, and those subjects silently
leave the analysis. Convert once, at the boundary, with
`Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0)`, which is true for the event whatever the
censoring codes are.
:::

### Analysis sets and the estimand

The SAP pre-specifies which [**analysis set**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-analysis-set) each analysis uses,
and ADSL implements the choice as flags. The intention-to-treat
(ITT) set, or full analysis set (FAS), includes every randomized
subject, analyzed as randomized (`ITTFL`, `FASFL`). A modified ITT
set excludes a few randomized subjects by a rule the protocol
states in advance (for example, no post-baseline assessment); its
definition varies by sponsor and must be read, not assumed. The
safety set includes every subject who received at least one dose,
analyzed as treated (`SAFFL`). A per-protocol set excludes
subjects with important protocol deviations (`PPROTFL`).

An analysis set is not the estimand's population. ICH E9(R1)
[@ich2019e9r1] defines the population at the level of the
scientific question, and the analysis set is chosen so that the
analysis estimates that estimand. For HF-HOME the SAP's estimand
uses a treatment-policy strategy for nonadherence
(@sec-analysis-plan-estimands): analyze every randomized subject
as randomized, from randomization. Filtering on the wrong flag
analyzes a different group of patients than the SAP promised, and
may no longer target the stated estimand.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The HF-HOME SAP's primary analysis is 'all
randomized patients, as randomized'. Which `ADSL` variables
implement that, and what changes if a programmer groups by
`TRT01A` instead?

**Answer.** Filter on `ITTFL == 'Y'` and group by `TRT01P`, the
planned (randomized) arm. Grouping by `TRT01A` moves every
nonadherent subject into the arm of the care they received, so the
groups are no longer the randomized groups and the comparison is
no longer protected by randomization; the treatment-policy
estimand is not what it estimates. The code runs either way, which
is why the specification names the variable.
:::

## Worked example: ADSL and ADTTE for HF-HOME {#sec-cdisc-worked}

The derivation below builds `ADSL` and an `ADTTE` for time to
readmission or death within 30 days of randomization, then
analyzes it on the ITT set. The SAP's primary analysis is the
30-day risk difference (@sec-analysis-plan-worked); the
time-to-event analysis here is supportive, describing when the
same composite events occurred.

### Derive ADSL

`ADSL` has exactly one row per subject and carries everything a
downstream analysis stratifies or filters on. Each date comes from
its proper source: `RANDDT` from the `RANDOMIZED` milestone in
`DS`; `TRTSDT` and `TRTEDT` from the first start and last end of
exposure in `EX`, never from the disposition date. Usual-care
subjects who received no home-health visit have no `EX` rows, so
their treatment dates are missing, which is correct.

```{r}
#| label: cdisc-adsl
randomized <- ds |>
  filter(DSDECOD == 'RANDOMIZED') |>
  transmute(USUBJID, RANDDT = as.Date(DSSTDTC))

exposure <- ex |>
  group_by(USUBJID) |>
  summarize(TRTSDT = min(as.Date(EXSTDTC)),
            TRTEDT = max(as.Date(EXENDTC)),
            .groups = 'drop')

arms <- c('Usual care', 'Home health')
adsl <- dm |>
  left_join(randomized, by = 'USUBJID',
            relationship = 'one-to-one', unmatched = 'error') |>
  left_join(exposure, by = 'USUBJID',
            relationship = 'one-to-one') |>
  mutate(
    TRT01P  = factor(ARM, levels = arms),
    TRT01A  = factor(ACTARM, levels = arms),
    AGEGR1  = if_else(AGE < 65, '<65', '>=65'),
    ITTFL   = if_else(!is.na(RANDDT), 'Y', 'N'),
    PPROTFL = if_else(TRT01A == TRT01P, 'Y', 'N')
  ) |>
  select(STUDYID, USUBJID, SUBJID, SITEID, AGE, AGEGR1, SEX, RACE,
         TRT01P, TRT01A, RANDDT, TRTSDT, TRTEDT, ITTFL, PPROTFL)

stopifnot(nrow(adsl) == nrow(dm), !anyDuplicated(adsl$USUBJID))
count(adsl, TRT01P, PPROTFL)
```

The per-protocol flag is included to show what it does, not to be
used: restricting HF-HOME to subjects who received their assigned
care compares two subsets selected after randomization, and
@sec-analysis-plan-estimands explains why that targets none of
the estimands the SAP could state.

### Derive ADTTE

`ADTTE` is a BDS dataset: one row per subject per time-to-event
parameter. The clock starts at `RANDDT`, because the estimand is
defined from randomization, and the home-health visit happens
after it or not at all. The event is the first of a readmission
(from `HO`) or a death (from `DS`) within 30 days. A subject
without an event is censored at day 30 (`CNSR = 1`), or, if lost
to follow-up, at the last contact (`CNSR = 2`).

```{r}
#| label: cdisc-adtte
disposition <- ds |>
  filter(DSCAT == 'DISPOSITION EVENT') |>
  transmute(USUBJID, DSDECOD, DISPDT = as.Date(DSSTDTC))

first_readmit <- ho |>
  group_by(USUBJID) |>
  summarize(READMDT = min(as.Date(HOSTDTC)), .groups = 'drop')

deaths <- disposition |>
  filter(DSDECOD == 'DEATH') |>
  transmute(USUBJID, DTHDT = DISPDT)

adtte <- adsl |>
  select(STUDYID, USUBJID, TRT01P, TRT01A, ITTFL, RANDDT) |>
  left_join(disposition, by = 'USUBJID',
            relationship = 'one-to-one', unmatched = 'error') |>
  left_join(first_readmit, by = 'USUBJID',
            relationship = 'one-to-one') |>
  left_join(deaths, by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one') |>
  mutate(
    PARAMCD  = 'RDTH30',
    PARAM    = 'Time to readmission or death within 30 days (days)',
    STARTDT  = RANDDT,
    EVNTDT   = pmin(READMDT, DTHDT, na.rm = TRUE),
    CNSR     = case_when(
      !is.na(EVNTDT) & EVNTDT <= STARTDT + 30 ~ 0L,
      DSDECOD == 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP'          ~ 2L,
      .default                                = 1L),
    ADT      = case_when(
      CNSR == 0L ~ EVNTDT,
      CNSR == 2L ~ pmin(DISPDT, STARTDT + 30),
      .default   = STARTDT + 30),
    AVAL     = as.numeric(ADT - STARTDT),
    EVNTDESC = case_when(
      CNSR == 0L & !is.na(READMDT) & EVNTDT == READMDT ~ 'READMISSION',
      CNSR == 0L ~ 'DEATH',
      CNSR == 2L ~ 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP',
      .default   = 'NO EVENT BY DAY 30')
  ) |>
  select(STUDYID, USUBJID, TRT01P, TRT01A, ITTFL, PARAMCD, PARAM,
         STARTDT, ADT, AVAL, CNSR, EVNTDESC)

stopifnot(nrow(adtte) == nrow(adsl),
          all(adtte$AVAL >= 0 & adtte$AVAL <= 30))
count(adtte, CNSR, EVNTDESC)
```

`AVAL` here is `ADT - STARTDT`; many sponsors add one day so that
an event on the start date has `AVAL = 1`. Either is defensible,
and the specification states which.[^aval]

[^aval]: The SAP and the ADaM specification should agree on this
    and on the censoring date for subjects lost to follow-up (last
    contact, here; some plans use the last date of known status).
    Neither choice changes the estimand; both change `AVAL`.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Re-derive the event count and the event days from the raw outcome
file, which never passed through SDTM, and compare.

```{r}
#| label: cdisc-adtte-verify
raw_events <- read_hf('outcomes.csv') |>
  filter(event_30d == 1) |>
  transmute(USUBJID = paste('HFHOME', patient_id, sep = '-'),
            days = days_to_event)
adtte_events <- adtte |>
  filter(CNSR == 0) |>
  select(USUBJID, days = AVAL)

stopifnot(
  nrow(raw_events) == nrow(adtte_events),
  isTRUE(all.equal(arrange(raw_events, USUBJID),
                   arrange(adtte_events, USUBJID),
                   check.attributes = FALSE))
)
nrow(adtte_events)
```

Two derivations from different sources that agree subject by
subject are evidence that the censoring logic is right; a count
that agrees and days that do not would point at the date logic.
:::

### Analyze from ADTTE

The analysis filters on the ITT flag and converts the censoring
code once, at the boundary, with `CNSR == 0`. HF-HOME's `ADTTE`
contains `CNSR = 2`, so this is not a matter of style: `1 - CNSR`
would drop the subjects lost to follow-up.

```{r}
#| label: cdisc-survival
analysis <- adtte |>
  filter(ITTFL == 'Y', PARAMCD == 'RDTH30')

fit <- survfit(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis)
summary(fit, times = 30)

cox <- coxph(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis)
hr <- summary(cox)$conf.int
hr
stopifnot(cox$n == nrow(analysis))
```

The hazard ratio for home health against usual care is
`r sprintf('%.2f', hr[1, 'exp(coef)'])` (95% confidence interval
`r sprintf('%.2f', hr[1, 'lower .95'])` to
`r sprintf('%.2f', hr[1, 'upper .95'])`). The interval includes 1,
so this supportive analysis, like the primary one, is
inconclusive: it neither shows that home health reduces early
readmission or death nor rules out a reduction of the size the
trial was designed to detect. The `stopifnot()` confirms that no
subject was dropped on the way into the model. @fig-cdisc-km shows
the cumulative incidence by arm, with the risk table that
regulatory reviewers expect beneath the curve.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cdisc-km
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative incidence of readmission or death within 30
#|   days of randomization, by randomized arm, from the HF-HOME
#|   ADTTE (ITT set). Shaded bands are pointwise 95% confidence
#|   intervals; the table beneath gives the number still at risk."
#| fig-alt: "Two rising step curves of cumulative incidence over 30
#|   days, one per randomized arm, with overlapping shaded
#|   confidence bands; the usual-care curve lies slightly above the
#|   home-health curve. A risk table beneath the axis lists the
#|   number of subjects still at risk in each arm at days 0, 10,
#|   20, and 30."
#| fig-scap: "Cumulative incidence from the HF-HOME ADTTE"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| message: false
library(survminer)

ggsurvplot(fit, data = analysis,
           fun          = 'event',
           conf.int     = TRUE,
           risk.table   = TRUE,
           break.time.by = 10,
           xlab         = 'Days from randomization',
           ylab         = 'Cumulative incidence',
           legend.title = 'Arm',
           legend.labs  = arms,
           ggtheme      = theme_minimal())
```

The row granularity changed at every step, and tracking it is the
skill: `dm` has one row per subject, `ex` one per home-health
visit, `ds` two per subject, `ho` one per readmission; `adsl`
returns to one per subject and `adtte` has one per subject per
parameter. The declared `relationship =` on every join and the
`stopifnot()` after each derivation are the minimum.

### Exercises

2. Stack a second parameter into `ADTTE`: time to death within 30
   days (`PARAMCD = 'DTH30'`), censored at day 30 or at last
   contact as before. Verify that the stacked dataset has two rows
   per subject and that its number of `DTH30` events equals the
   number of `DEATH` records in `DS`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-19-2
adtte_dth <- adsl |>
  select(STUDYID, USUBJID, TRT01P, TRT01A, ITTFL, RANDDT) |>
  left_join(disposition, by = 'USUBJID',
            relationship = 'one-to-one', unmatched = 'error') |>
  left_join(deaths, by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one') |>
  mutate(
    PARAMCD  = 'DTH30',
    PARAM    = 'Time to death within 30 days (days)',
    STARTDT  = RANDDT,
    CNSR     = case_when(
      !is.na(DTHDT)                  ~ 0L,
      DSDECOD == 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP' ~ 2L,
      .default                       = 1L),
    ADT      = case_when(
      CNSR == 0L ~ DTHDT,
      CNSR == 2L ~ pmin(DISPDT, STARTDT + 30),
      .default   = STARTDT + 30),
    AVAL     = as.numeric(ADT - STARTDT),
    EVNTDESC = case_when(
      CNSR == 0L ~ 'DEATH',
      CNSR == 2L ~ 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP',
      .default   = 'NO EVENT BY DAY 30')
  ) |>
  select(all_of(names(adtte)))

adtte2 <- bind_rows(adtte, adtte_dth)
stopifnot(
  nrow(adtte2) == 2 * nrow(adsl),
  all(count(adtte2, USUBJID)$n == 2),
  sum(adtte2$PARAMCD == 'DTH30' & adtte2$CNSR == 0) ==
    sum(ds$DSDECOD == 'DEATH')
)
count(adtte2, PARAMCD, CNSR)
```

BDS datasets grow downward: a second endpoint is more rows with a
different `PARAMCD`, never a second `AVAL` column.
`select(all_of(names(adtte)))` keeps the two blocks stackable;
`bind_rows()` of frames with different columns succeeds and fills
the gaps with `NA`, which is how a BDS dataset quietly acquires
columns that apply to one parameter only. Deaths are a subset of
the composite events, so the `DTH30` event count must be smaller
than the `RDTH30` count; deaths after a readmission are events
here and not there.
:::

3. Build a minimal BDS `ADLB` for NT-proBNP (N-terminal
   pro-B-type natriuretic peptide) from `labs.csv` and
   `visits.csv`: one row per subject per analysis visit
   (`AVISIT` of `'BASELINE'` for discharge and `'DAY 30'` for the
   day-30 clinic), with `AVAL`, `ABLFL`, `BASE`, and `CHG`.
   Restrict it to randomized subjects, and assert one row per
   subject and visit.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-19-3
visit_map <- read_hf('visits.csv') |>
  filter(visit_type %in% c('discharge', 'clinic_day30')) |>
  select(visit_id, visit_type)

adlb <- read_hf('labs.csv') |>
  filter(test_code == 'NTPROBNP') |>
  distinct(patient_id, visit_id, test_code, value) |>
  inner_join(visit_map, by = 'visit_id',
             relationship = 'one-to-one') |>
  transmute(USUBJID = paste('HFHOME', patient_id, sep = '-'),
            PARAMCD = 'NTPROBNP',
            AVISIT  = if_else(visit_type == 'discharge',
                              'BASELINE', 'DAY 30'),
            AVAL    = value) |>
  semi_join(adsl, by = 'USUBJID') |>
  group_by(USUBJID) |>
  mutate(ABLFL = if_else(AVISIT == 'BASELINE', 'Y', NA_character_),
         BASE  = AVAL[AVISIT == 'BASELINE'][1],
         CHG   = if_else(AVISIT == 'BASELINE', NA_real_,
                         AVAL - BASE)) |>
  ungroup()

stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(adlb[c('USUBJID', 'AVISIT')]),
          all(adlb$USUBJID %in% adsl$USUBJID))
count(adlb, AVISIT)
```

Two planted defects meet this derivation. The exact duplicate of
one discharge NT-proBNP row is removed by `distinct()` on all
columns, which is safe only because the rows are identical; the
assertion after it would catch a conflicting pair. The orphan
patient `2433` has labs but no visit record, so the inner join to
`visits` already drops it; the `semi_join()` to `ADSL` states the
rule that guarantees it, because ADaM contains randomized subjects
only. `ABLFL` is `'Y'` or missing,
never `'N'`, as for every ADaM flag of this kind.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does the HF-HOME `ADTTE` start the clock at
`RANDDT` rather than `TRTSDT`?

**Answer.** Because the estimand is defined for every randomized
subject from randomization, and `TRTSDT` (the first home-health
visit) is missing for most usual-care subjects and comes after
randomization for the rest. Starting at `TRTSDT` would drop or
shift exactly the subjects whose care differed from assignment,
and the comparison would no longer be between randomized groups.
:::

## Industry practice: tables, validation, double programming {#sec-cdisc-industry}

### The pharmaverse

Until the late 2010s, almost all ADaM work in industry was done in
SAS (@sec-sas). Since about 2022, the year `admiral`
[@mancini2026admiral] first reached CRAN (the Comprehensive R
Archive Network), a cross-company collaboration called the
[**pharmaverse**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-pharmaverse) has produced R packages for each step of the
pipeline: `admiral` for ADaM derivations, `metacore` and
`metatools` to read and apply specifications, and `xportr` to
write the SAS transport (XPT) files the FDA requires. At a sponsor
that has adopted R, expect these in production.

### Tables, listings, and figures

Every table in a CSR is built from ADaM, and several R packages
build them. `gtsummary` [@sjoberg2021gtsummary] is the general
one; the demographics table below is computed from `ADSL`.

```{r}
#| label: cdisc-table1
#| message: false
library(gtsummary)

adsl |>
  filter(ITTFL == 'Y') |>
  select(TRT01P, AGE, AGEGR1, SEX) |>
  tbl_summary(by = TRT01P,
              label = list(AGE ~ 'Age, years',
                           AGEGR1 ~ 'Age group', SEX ~ 'Sex')) |>
  add_overall()
```

Two families are built for regulatory output. `rtables`, with the
analysis functions of `tern`, describes a table as a layout that
is then applied to the data; `Tplyr` builds a table from layers of
counts and descriptive statistics. Neither is installed in this
book's environment, so the code is display-only and unverified
here:

```r
library(rtables)
library(tern)
basic_table() |>
  split_cols_by('TRT01P') |>
  add_overall_col('All') |>
  analyze_vars(c('AGE', 'SEX')) |>
  build_table(adsl)

library(Tplyr)
tplyr_table(adsl, TRT01P) |>
  add_layer(group_desc(AGE)) |>
  add_layer(group_count(SEX)) |>
  build()
```

### Publication and submission tables: shells and mocks

The `gtsummary` demographics table above was built in one `tbl_summary()`
call against whichever columns of `ADSL` seemed useful to look at. That
is appropriate for exploration, and for the many tables a biostatistician
builds while checking a dataset or drafting a manuscript. It is not how
the tables of a clinical study report are built, and the difference is
not the software; it is what exists before anyone writes code.

A CSR table, listing, or figure (collectively, a TLF) is built against a
**shell**: a specification of the table's title, its population, every
row and row group, every column and column header, the footnotes, the
decimal rules, and often the exact page layout, agreed and signed off by
the biostatistician and the lead statistical programmer before the
database is locked. The shell is part of the TLF specification that
accompanies the SAP, numbered so that every reviewer, from the sponsor's
own QC programmer to an FDA statistical reviewer reading the final CSR,
can find 'Table 14.2.1' and know in advance what it will contain and
what it will not. Nothing about the shell depends on what the data turn
out to show. That is the point: a reviewer who sees the primary efficacy
table laid out one way in the SAP and a different way in the CSR has
reason to ask whether the second table was shaped by a look at the
results, which is exactly the appearance a pre-specified shell exists to
avoid.

A **mock** is the shell filled with placeholder values, typeset and
reviewed before the data exist or before they are unblinded, to confirm
that the layout reads correctly, that long row labels do not wrap badly,
and that the table fits a printed page the way the shell's author
imagined. A mock for HF-HOME's composite-endpoint table might look like
this, with every number a placeholder:

```
Table 14.2.1  Supportive Analysis: Time to 30-Day Readmission or Death
              (Intention-to-Treat Population)

                                Usual care     Home health
                                (N=xxx)        (N=xxx)
  Subjects with event, n (%)    xx (xx.x%)     xx (xx.x%)
  Hazard ratio (95% CI)                    x.xx (x.xx, x.xx)
  Log-rank p-value                              x.xxx

Program: adtte.R / tlf-14-2-1.R    Output generated: ddMONyyyy hh:mm
```

Once the shell and mock are signed off, the programmer implements the
layout in code, and the layout, not the programmer's judgment at
table-building time, decides what appears. In `tern`, the shell becomes
a `rtables` layout: the column split, the row-generating functions, and
their order are fixed once, and the same layout code is applied to
whatever data a given run provides. In `Tplyr`, the shell becomes a
sequence of layers, each one a row group (`group_desc()` for a
continuous summary, `group_count()` for a categorical one), added in the
order the shell specifies. Neither package lets the real numbers
rearrange the table; a hazard ratio of 1.3 and a hazard ratio of 0.6
print into the same cell, because the cell was fixed before either
number existed. A sketch of HF-HOME's table in `tern`, display-only
because the package is not installed in this book's environment:

```r
library(rtables)
library(tern)

lyt <- basic_table(
    title = 'Table 14.2.1  Supportive Analysis: Time to 30-Day
             Readmission or Death (Intention-to-Treat Population)',
    subtitles = 'Cox proportional hazards model, usual care as
                 reference'
  ) |>
  split_cols_by('TRT01P') |>
  add_colcounts() |>
  analyze_vars('CNSR', afun = s_proportion,
               .stats = 'n_prop') |>
  summarize_coxreg(variables = list(tte = 'AVAL', is_event = 'event'),
                    control = control_coxreg())

build_table(lyt, adtte)
```

The shell this code implements is identical, row for row, to the mock
above; what changes between a dry run on placeholder data and the
locked-data run is only the numbers the layout computes, never the rows
or columns that appear. This is also why a shell is reviewed so early:
a row the SAP's analysis does not support, or a row the shell omits
that the SAP requires, is a cheap fix before any code exists and an
expensive one once a locked dataset's TLFs are already being QC'd
against it.

Two further conventions follow from the shell existing at all. First,
the exact column structure, including column order, the definition of
any 'Total' or 'Overall' column, and whether a column reports counts,
percentages, or both, is part of the shell and is never a programmer's
choice at build time; two programmers building the same shell from the
same data must produce column-identical tables even before double
programming compares the numbers inside them. Second, the shell commits
to a population and an analysis before the shell's author has seen any
outcome data, which is a weaker but related form of the pre-specification
this book has argued for throughout: an estimand and an analysis plan
fixed before results exist cannot be reshaped by what the results turn
out to be (@sec-analysis-plan-estimands).

The same shell discipline governs listings and figures, the other two
letters of 'TLF', not only tables. A listing is a shell too, specifying
exactly which SDTM or ADaM variables appear, in what order, sorted by
what key, with what footnotes about truncation or suppression of
confidential fields; a figure's shell specifies the plot type, axes,
legend, and any reference lines, the way `ggsurvplot()`'s arguments
above fix the axis labels and the arm legend before any data are
plotted. A Kaplan-Meier figure built once as part of exploratory
analysis and a CSR figure built from the same `fit` object can differ
only in presentation discipline, not in the statistics, if the shell
that specifies the CSR figure's axes and legend was agreed in advance
and the code that builds it, display-only or not, implements that shell
exactly.

TLFs are QC'd the same way ADaM datasets are: a second programmer, often
using a different package or a simpler ad hoc script, independently
reproduces the numbers inside the shell and compares them to the
primary output, cell by cell, the same discipline as the `diffdf`
comparison in @sec-cdisc-industry applied to a table instead of a
dataset. A `gtsummary` table built quickly from the locked data is a
reasonable independent check on a `tern` table's numbers, precisely
because the two packages compute the summary statistics by different
code paths from the same shell's row and column definitions; agreement
between them is evidence about the numbers, while agreement between two
runs of the same `tern` layout is evidence about nothing new, for the
same reason a second run of identical code added nothing to the ADaM
double-programming check earlier in this chapter.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Before trusting a built TLF, check it against its own shell line by
line: same title text, same column headers in the same order, same row
labels in the same order, same footnotes. A table that computes the
right numbers in the wrong shell is still a finding to fix, because the
shell is itself a reviewed, agreed artifact.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A programmer builds the primary efficacy table, notices
that a 'Difference in proportions' row would make the comparison
clearer, and adds it. The added row is correctly computed. What is
wrong?

**Answer.** The row was not in the shell the biostatistician and the
lead programmer signed off on. Adding it, even correctly, means the
table that reaches the SAP's reviewers and ultimately FDA differs from
the one that was specified and agreed before the data were seen, which
is exactly the appearance of data-driven table-building that a
pre-specified shell exists to rule out. The right process is to propose
the row as a shell change, get it reviewed and signed off, and only then
implement it; a good idea discovered while coding is still a
specification change, not a coding decision.
:::

### Exercises

4. Sketch a shell, as a plain-text mock like the one above, for a TLF
   reporting HF-HOME's NT-proBNP change from baseline to day 30
   (`ADLB`, from the worked example's exercise 3) by randomized arm.
   Decide, and state explicitly, what the shell's footnotes should
   disclose about missing day-30 values, since @sec-cdisc-worked's
   `ADLB` has no row for a subject who lacks a day-30 measurement.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A minimal shell:

```
Table 14.x.x  Change from Baseline in NT-proBNP to Day 30
              (Intention-to-Treat Population)

                              Usual care      Home health
                              (N=xxx)         (N=xxx)
  Baseline, mean (SD)         xxx.x (xx.xx)   xxx.x (xx.xx)
  Day 30, mean (SD)           xxx.x (xx.xx)   xxx.x (xx.xx)
  Change, mean (SD)           xxx.x (xx.xx)   xxx.x (xx.xx)
  n with day-30 value         xxx             xxx

Footnote: Subjects without a day-30 NT-proBNP measurement are excluded
from the day-30 and change rows; the denominator for each row is
stated as n, not N, to make this explicit.
```

The key decision is the footnote: `ADLB` as built in the worked
example has one row per subject per visit actually measured, so a
subject missing the day-30 draw contributes no day-30 row and no
`CHG` value, rather than an explicit missing-data code. A shell that
reports only `N` in the header without an `n` row for each statistic
would let a reader assume the change row was computed on every
randomized subject, which it was not; the footnote is the shell's way
of pre-committing to disclosing that gap rather than leaving a
programmer to decide, after seeing how much data is missing, whether
it is worth mentioning.
:::

### R in submissions and validated packages

R is accepted in submissions. The R Consortium's R Submissions
Working Group has run pilot submissions to FDA built in R. Pilot
1, four TLFs, received FDA's final review response in March 2022;
Pilot 2, a Shiny application, received its response in September
2023; Pilot 3, ADaM datasets and TLFs built in R, received its
final response letter in August 2024; and Pilot 4, the Shiny
application delivered through WebAssembly and through a
container, received FDA's review letter in May 2026.[^pilots]
These are test submissions, not drug approvals. What a sponsor must
show is that the software it relies on is fit for purpose. The R
Validation Hub, another R Consortium working group, publishes a
risk-based approach to that question, and its `riskmetric` package
scores a package on documentation, testing, maintenance, and use
(display-only; not installed here):

```r
library(riskmetric)
pkg_ref('survival') |>
  pkg_assess() |>
  pkg_score()
```

As of this writing, `riskmetric` is maintenance-only: the Validation
Hub has moved its development effort to a successor, `val.meter`,
and directs feature requests there. Bug reports for `riskmetric`
itself are still accepted. Check both packages' status before
adopting either.

[^pilots]: As of 2026-10. Dates are from the working group's
    pilot pages (`rconsortium.github.io/submissions-wg`), the
    pilot repositories on GitHub (`github.com/RConsortium`), and
    R Consortium announcements of August 2024 (Pilot 3) and May
    2026 (Pilot 4). Pilot 5 replaces XPT with Dataset-JSON: it was
    submitted to FDA in fall 2025, FDA requested minor rework, and
    the team resubmitted in January 2026, with completion hoped for
    spring 2026. Check the working group's pilot pages for the
    current status before citing a result.

### Double programming

The standard validation of an ADaM dataset or a table in industry
is [**double programming**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-double-programming): a second programmer derives the same
output independently from the specification, without reading the
first programmer's code, and the two outputs are compared value by
value. Any difference is investigated until both agree or the
specification is clarified. The `diffdf` package is the usual
comparison tool in R (display-only; not installed here):

```r
diffdf::diffdf(base = adtte, compare = adtte_qc, keys = 'USUBJID')
```

The chunk below is the same idea with tools already loaded: an
independent derivation of the whole `ADTTE`, from the raw CSV
files rather than from SDTM, compared row by row.

```{r}
#| label: cdisc-double-programming
last_contact <- read_hf('visits.csv') |>
  group_by(patient_id) |>
  summarize(last_day = max(visit_day), .groups = 'drop')

adtte_qc <- read_hf('outcomes.csv') |>
  left_join(last_contact, by = 'patient_id',
            relationship = 'one-to-one') |>
  transmute(
    USUBJID = paste('HFHOME', patient_id, sep = '-'),
    AVAL = case_when(event_30d == 1 ~ days_to_event,
                     !ascertained   ~ pmin(last_day, 30),
                     .default       = 30),
    CNSR = case_when(event_30d == 1 ~ 0L,
                     !ascertained   ~ 2L,
                     .default       = 1L)
  ) |>
  arrange(USUBJID)

primary <- adtte |>
  select(USUBJID, AVAL, CNSR) |>
  arrange(USUBJID)

mismatches <- primary |>
  inner_join(adtte_qc, by = 'USUBJID', suffix = c('', '_qc'),
             relationship = 'one-to-one', unmatched = 'error') |>
  filter(AVAL != AVAL_qc | CNSR != CNSR_qc)
stopifnot(nrow(mismatches) == 0)
nrow(mismatches)
```

The QC derivation shares no code and no intermediate dataset with
the primary one: it uses `visits.csv` for the last contact where
the primary used the `DS` date, and the outcome flags where the
primary used `HO` and `DS`. Agreement on all
`r nrow(primary)` subjects is evidence about the derivation; a
second run of the same code would be evidence about nothing.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
An independent re-derivation by a model is the AI analogue of
double programming, and it has the same rule: the second
derivation must not see the first.

> **Context.** I am validating an ADaM `ADTTE` dataset. The
> specification is below: [the `ADTTE` rows of the ADaM
> specification, with each variable's source and derivation].
> The source files are described by these variable lists and
> types: [column names and types of `outcomes.csv` and
> `visits.csv`, and three synthetic rows of each].
>
> **Constraints.** Write an R function that derives `USUBJID`,
> `AVAL`, and `CNSR` from the two source files using `dplyr`
> only. Use `CNSR = 0` for the event and the positive codes in
> the specification for censoring. Declare `relationship =` on
> every join. Do not ask for, and do not use, any existing
> derivation code.
>
> **Criteria.** List every assumption you make where the
> specification is silent (the censoring date for a subject lost
> to follow-up, the treatment of a death after a readmission).
> I will compare your output to the primary dataset subject by
> subject.

*Failure mode.* A model shown the primary code reproduces its
errors, which defeats the comparison; a model not shown the
specification invents a censoring rule, often `CNSR = 1` for
every censored subject. *Check.* Run its function on the real
files inside your environment and compare with the
`mismatches` join above, which must return no rows; investigate
every assumption it listed against the SAP. Real SDTM and ADaM are
individual patient data and the sponsor's confidential
information: send the specification and synthetic rows, never the
datasets (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A programmer validates an `ADTTE` by re-running the
primary program on a second machine and comparing outputs. They
agree exactly. What has been shown?

**Answer.** That the program is deterministic, not that it is
correct. Double programming is valuable because the second
derivation is independent: different code, written from the
specification by someone who has not seen the first, so that a
shared misreading is unlikely. A misread censoring rule survives
any number of re-runs of the same code.
:::

## Regulated-industry computing {#sec-cdisc-regulated}

Double programming (@sec-cdisc-industry) is evidence about one dataset.
Two further layers of rule govern the computing environment that
produces every dataset and table in a submission: a US regulation on
what counts as a trustworthy electronic record, and an international
guideline on how a sponsor manages the risk that its computerized
systems, R and its packages among them, introduce into a trial's data.
A biostatistician who only ever sees SAS or R code will still meet both,
usually at a sponsor's own standard operating procedures (SOPs), which
exist to implement them.

### 21 CFR Part 11: electronic records and electronic signatures

Title 21, Part 11 of the US Code of Federal Regulations
[@fda1997part11] sets the conditions under which the FDA accepts
electronic records and electronic signatures as equivalent to paper
records and handwritten signatures. It does not, by itself, require
that any particular record be kept; it applies once a sponsor chooses
to keep, in electronic form, a record that some other FDA regulation
(the 'predicate rule') already requires, for instance the clinical data
underlying a new drug application. Three obligations matter most to a
statistician or programmer who works inside a system built to satisfy
Part 11.

**Audit trails.** A system covered by Part 11 must generate a
computer-generated, time-stamped audit trail that records who created,
modified, or deleted a record, and when, without obscuring the earlier
entries. For an ADaM dataset this means the specification, the
programs, and the dataset itself typically live in a validated system
(a clinical trial management system or a controlled document and code
repository) that logs every change, rather than in a shared folder
where a file can be silently overwritten. A `git` history is a step in
this direction but is not, by itself, a Part 11 audit trail: Part 11
requires the trail to be part of a controlled, access-restricted system
with its own retention guarantees, which plain version control does not
provide on its own.

**Access controls.** Only authorized individuals may operate the
system, each identified by a unique credential, with access rights set
by role (read-only reviewer, programmer with write access to a
particular study, and so on). A programmer who shares a login with a
colleague, even briefly, breaks the link between the audit trail's
record of 'who' and the person who actually acted, which is the
specific guarantee Part 11 is built to provide.

**Record retention.** Records kept to satisfy a predicate rule must
remain retrievable, and reproducible in a readable form, for the
retention period that rule specifies, which can run well beyond a
study's active life and beyond the working life of the software that
produced the record. A sponsor's SOPs for archiving an R environment,
down to the package versions a study used, exist to keep that promise
when R itself, or a package on CRAN, has moved on.

**Electronic signatures.** Where a signature is required (sign-off on a
SAP, approval of a locked dataset, release of a CSR), Part 11 requires
that the signature be uniquely linked to one individual, never reused
or reassigned to someone else, and applied only by its genuine owner,
typically through a two-component mechanism such as a credential plus a
password or token. A biostatistician's electronic approval of an ADaM
specification inside a controlled document system is the Part 11
analogue of a wet signature on a paper memo, and carries the same legal
weight once the system itself meets the regulation.

Part 11 is US-specific and narrower than it sounds: it is a rule about
what makes an *electronic* record acceptable in place of a paper one,
not a general statement of what good computing practice looks like. The
broader question, of how much validation and control a given
computerized system needs, is addressed by ICH guidance.

These obligations are not abstractions for a biostatistician who never
touches a validated system directly. An FDA inspection of a study site
or sponsor, conducted under the agency's Bioresearch Monitoring (BIMO)
program, can and does ask to see the audit trail behind a reported
result: who changed a value in the clinical database, when, and under
whose approval a locked dataset was released for analysis. A derivation
that exists only as an interactive session typed at a console, with no
record of who ran it or when, is not what Part 11 or a sponsor's SOPs
describing it will accept as the basis for a submitted result, however
correct the derivation's numbers turn out to be; the record of how a
result was produced is treated as part of the evidence for the result,
not an afterthought to it.

### ICH E6(R3): data governance and computerized systems

ICH E6 is the Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guideline, revised twice
since its original 1996 text; the third revision, E6(R3), reached ICH
Step 4 (the point at which the ICH Assembly adopts the final text and
recommends it to its member regulatory authorities) on 6 January 2025,
with the European Medicines Agency's Step 5 adoption of the principles
and Annex 1 taking effect on 23 July 2025 [@ich2025e6r3]. As of this
writing, Annex 2 of E6(R3) is on a later timetable; check the ICH
database for the current status before citing a date for it.

E6(R3)'s most consequential change for a statistician or programmer is
not a new form to fill out; it is a shift to **risk-based quality
management**, applied explicitly to computerized systems. Rather than
prescribing a fixed checklist for every system regardless of what it
does, the guideline asks the sponsor to identify what could go wrong
with a given system's data (a wrong randomization code, a corrupted
export, an unvalidated calculation silently feeding a reported result)
and to scale the system's validation, access control, and documentation
to the size and likelihood of that risk. A sponsor's own patient
randomization system warrants more scrutiny than a read-only reporting
dashboard built on already-locked data, and E6(R3) asks the sponsor to
be able to show that it reasoned this way, not merely that it applied
one uniform procedure to both.

Regulators and industry commonly summarize the resulting data-integrity
expectations with the mnemonic ALCOA+: data should be attributable,
legible, contemporaneous, original, and accurate (the original ALCOA),
and, as elaborated since, complete, consistent, enduring, and available.
E6(R3) does not use this acronym in its own text, but its data
governance expectations (traceable changes, protection against
unauthorized alteration, and systems fit for their intended use) align
with it, and the mnemonic is a convenient checklist against which to
read a sponsor's data-management SOPs.

Part 11 and E6(R3) are not redundant. Part 11 is a US rule about when an
electronic record substitutes for a paper one; E6(R3) is an
international guideline about how a sponsor manages the quality of a
clinical trial, of which the integrity of its computerized systems is
one part. A sponsor operating a Part 11-compliant system has satisfied
one specific US requirement; it has not, by that fact alone, satisfied
E6(R3)'s broader expectation that the system's validation effort was
scaled to its risk and documented as such. A global sponsor running a
multinational trial needs to show both.

### Validating R packages for regulated use

Under a risk-based framework, R itself, and every package an analysis
depends on, is a computerized system whose risk to the trial's data
must be assessed and, where warranted, mitigated. Re-deriving that
assessment from first principles for every study would be wasteful, and
it is not what sponsors that use R actually do. The R Validation Hub,
the R Consortium working group already introduced in
@sec-cdisc-industry for `riskmetric` and its successor `val.meter`, is
the industry's shared answer to this question for R: assess a package
once per environment (its test coverage, its maintenance activity, the
stability of its exported interface, the size of its user base) and
reuse that assessment, documented, across the studies that run in the
same validated environment, rather than re-justifying the choice of
`survival::coxph()` in every SAP.

This is the connection worth making explicit. Double programming
(@sec-cdisc-industry) is per-analysis evidence: it shows that this
dataset's derivation, run against this study's source data, reproduces
independently. Package risk assessment is per-environment evidence: it
shows that the software both derivations relied on behaves as its
documentation claims, before either derivation is attempted. Neither
substitutes for the other. A correctly validated copy of `survival`
run with a transposed censoring code still produces the wrong curve
(@sec-cdisc-adam); and a brilliant, independently double-programmed
derivation built on a package that silently drops `NA` rows from a
join is still wrong for a reason double programming alone will not
surface, because both programmers may make the same assumption about
the package. A sponsor's R validation SOP and the study team's double
programming plan are two different controls, addressed at two different
layers of risk, and both are expected.

The practical effect for a programmer joining such a sponsor is a
validated environment rather than a free choice of package versions: an
`renv.lock` (@sec-renv) pinned to a specific, already-assessed set of
package versions, changed only through a controlled process that
re-triggers the relevant risk assessment, rather than upgraded package
by package whenever a newer CRAN release appears. This can feel like
friction to someone used to running `renv::update()` freely, but it is
the same logic as SDTM's immutability (@sec-cdisc-pipeline): a result
traced to a package version that the validation record no longer
describes is a result whose computational basis can no longer be
reconstructed, which is precisely the failure E6(R3)'s risk-based
framework and Part 11's retention requirement are both written to
prevent.

### eSubmission mechanics: eCTD and pkglite

The datasets, programs, and Define-XML discussed earlier in this
chapter (@sec-cdisc-pipeline) are not emailed to FDA as a folder of
files; they are assembled into the electronic Common Technical Document
(eCTD), the standardized, XML-backboned folder structure that ICH
regions require for a regulatory submission. At a high level, an eCTD
submission is organized into five numbered modules: Module 1 holds
region-specific administrative information; Modules 2 through 4 hold
the Common Technical Document summaries, quality, and nonclinical
information; and Module 5 holds the clinical study reports, including,
for each study, its datasets, its ADaM and SDTM metadata (Define-XML),
and its analysis programs, in a defined subfolder structure. A
submission is built incrementally over a product's life cycle, with
each later submission adding or replacing eCTD 'leaves' rather than
restarting the folder from scratch, which is part of why the ADRG and
SDRG (@tbl-cdisc-package) exist as narrative guides to what changed and
why. Within Module 5, a study's materials sit under a folder keyed to
its study identifier, with conventional subfolders separating the
datasets themselves from the programs that produced them (`datasets/`
and `analysis/programs/`, in the naming most sponsors have converged
on, though the eCTD standard itself does not mandate these exact
names); Define-XML lives beside the datasets it describes, so a
reviewer opening the study folder can move from a variable's entry in
Define-XML to the dataset that contains it and, where provided, to the
program that derived it, without leaving the submission's own folder
structure.

The eCTD's file-format rules have historically been a poor fit for R
source code: FDA's eCTD gateway accepted a restricted list of file
types, and a source R package, with its nested `R/`, `man/`, `tests/`,
and `data/` subdirectories, did not sit comfortably inside a single
accepted leaf. `pkglite` [@zhang2026pkglite] was built at Merck to
solve exactly this problem: it collates a package's source files into
one or a small number of plain-text files, in a documented, lossless
format, that pack back into the original package structure with a
single call. A programmer preparing an R package for inclusion in an
eCTD submission (display-only; not installed here) collates the
package using the `file_ectd()` specification, which selects the files
an eCTD submission expects, then packs the result into a single text
file:

```r
library(pkglite)

collate(pkg = 'path/to/mypackage', file_ectd()) |>
  pack(output = 'mypackage.txt')
```

A reviewer, or the original team at a later submission, restores the
package from that text file with `unpack()`. As of this writing, the
R Consortium reports that FDA has since expanded the file formats its
eCTD portal accepts for R, so a sponsor can in some cases submit a
non-public R package directly as a `.zip` archive; `pkglite`'s
plain-text, line-by-line output remains useful on its own terms,
independent of what the gateway accepts, because a text file is
readable, diffable, and version-controllable in a way a zipped binary
archive is not, which matters for a reviewer trying to see what changed
between two submitted versions of a package.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Treating Part 11 compliance as sufficient for a computerized system's
regulatory standing.** A system can generate a flawless, tamper-evident
audit trail and still be running an unvalidated, undocumented R package
whose output no one has assessed for risk. Part 11 governs the
*record*, not the *software* that produced it; satisfying one says
nothing about having satisfied the other, and a sponsor's own
validation SOPs, not Part 11 itself, are what close that gap.
:::

### Exercises

5. HF-HOME's `ADTTE` derivation in this chapter relies on `dplyr` and
   `survival`. Using the risk factors the R Validation Hub's approach
   considers (test coverage, maintenance activity, interface
   stability, and size of the user base, as introduced in
   @sec-cdisc-industry), write two or three sentences arguing which of
   the two packages likely carries the lower risk to a submission, and
   what evidence you would want to see before accepting that
   assessment.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 5'}
A plausible argument, not a settled fact: `survival` has shipped with
base R's recommended package set for decades, has an exceptionally
large user base, and changes its exported interface rarely, all of
which argue for lower risk under the Hub's framework. That argument is
only as good as its evidence, though; the right next step is not to
assert it but to check, for the two packages' versions actually pinned
in the study's `renv.lock`, their CRAN check status, their last
release date, and their test coverage (for instance with `covr`), which
is what a `riskmetric` or `val.meter` run (@sec-cdisc-industry) is
built to summarize rather than leaving to intuition.
:::

6. A sponsor's SOP requires that every ADaM program be reviewed and
   electronically approved before the dataset it produces is released
   for TLF generation. List the Part 11 obligation that this approval
   step satisfies, and the ICH E6(R3) obligation (distinct from Part
   11) that justifies requiring the review in the first place.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 6'}
The electronic approval itself, if it uniquely identifies the approver
and cannot be reassigned or reused by someone else, satisfies Part
11's electronic-signature requirement. The requirement to review the
program *before* release is not a Part 11 obligation at all; Part 11
is silent on what a sponsor must review, only on what makes an
electronic record and signature acceptable once a review happens. The
review requirement itself follows from E6(R3)'s risk-based
quality-management expectation: a program that derives a reported
ADaM variable is a computerized-system output with real risk to data
integrity, and the SOP's review step is the control a sponsor has
chosen to manage that risk before the output is trusted downstream.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence; derived data are a build
   product.** SDTM is never edited; every analytic decision
   becomes an ADaM variable with a documented derivation.
2. **Habit 6: count before and after every join.** One row per
   subject in `ADSL`, one per subject per parameter in `ADTTE`;
   declare the relationship and assert the counts at every step.
3. **Habit 9: test the statistics, not the shape.** A dataset with
   the right columns can carry the wrong censoring; an independent
   derivation compared value by value is the test.

## Cumulative practice

7. *Cumulative (uses @sec-analysis-plan).* Write the ADaM
   specification for the HF-HOME `ADTTE` as a table with one row
   per variable (name, label, type, source, derivation), with the
   derivations stated so that a second programmer could implement
   them without this chapter's code. Then assert in R that every
   variable in `adtte` appears in your specification and no
   specification row is missing from `adtte`.
8. *On your own work (no key).* Install `admiral` and
   `pharmaverseadam`, and compare `pharmaverseadam::adsl` with the
   `ADSL` built here. List the variables that the simplified
   version lacks, and for each, say which analysis would need it.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 7'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-19-7
adtte_spec <- tribble(
  ~variable,  ~label,                           ~source,
  'STUDYID',  'Study identifier',               'ADSL.STUDYID',
  'USUBJID',  'Unique subject identifier',      'ADSL.USUBJID',
  'TRT01P',   'Planned treatment',              'ADSL.TRT01P',
  'TRT01A',   'Actual treatment',               'ADSL.TRT01A',
  'ITTFL',    'ITT population flag',            'ADSL.ITTFL',
  'PARAMCD',  'Parameter code',                 'Assigned',
  'PARAM',    'Parameter',                      'Assigned',
  'STARTDT',  'Time-to-event origin date',      'ADSL.RANDDT',
  'ADT',      'Analysis date',                  'HO.HOSTDTC, DS.DSSTDTC',
  'AVAL',     'Analysis value (days)',          'ADT - STARTDT',
  'CNSR',     'Censor (0 = event)',             'HO, DS',
  'EVNTDESC', 'Event or censoring description', 'HO, DS'
)
stopifnot(setequal(adtte_spec$variable, names(adtte)))
adtte_spec
```

A full specification adds a type and a derivation column; the
derivation for `CNSR`, for instance, reads '0 if the first of
`HO.HOSTDTC` (readmission) or `DS.DSSTDTC` where
`DS.DSDECOD = 'DEATH'` falls within 30 days of `STARTDT`; 2 if
`DS.DSDECOD = 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP'`; otherwise 1'. The `setequal()`
check is a structural check: it confirms that the specification
and the dataset name the same variables, not that the derivations
agree. The double-programming comparison in @sec-cdisc-industry is
the check on the values.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Variable | Dataset | Meaning | Trap |
|---|---|---|---|
| `USUBJID` | All | Unique subject identifier, study-wide | Join on it, never on `SUBJID` alone |
| `TRT01P`, `TRT01A` | ADSL | Planned and actual treatment, period 1 | As-randomized analyses use `TRT01P` |
| `RANDDT` | ADSL | Randomization date, from `DS` | The origin for ITT time-to-event |
| `TRTSDT`, `TRTEDT` | ADSL | First and last exposure, from `EX` | Not from the disposition date |
| `ITTFL`, `FASFL` | ADSL | Randomized, analyzed as randomized | The set is not the estimand's population |
| `SAFFL` | ADSL | Received any treatment, analyzed as treated | Not an efficacy set |
| `PPROTFL` | ADSL | No important protocol deviations | Selected after randomization |
| `PARAMCD`, `PARAM` | BDS | Parameter code (8 characters at most) and name | New endpoint, new rows |
| `AVAL`, `AVALC` | BDS | Analysis value, numeric and character | Units belong in `PARAM` |
| `AVISIT`, `AVISITN` | BDS | Analysis visit, character and numeric | Not the collected `VISIT` |
| `ABLFL`, `BASE`, `CHG` | BDS | Baseline flag, baseline value, change | Flags are `'Y'` or missing, never `'N'` |
| `STARTDT`, `ADT` | ADTTE | Origin and event or censoring date | `AVAL` convention: with or without `+ 1` |
| `CNSR` | ADTTE | 0 = event; positive = censored, by reason | `Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0)` |
| `EVNTDESC` | ADTTE | Event or censoring description | Must agree with `CNSR` |
| `ANL01FL` | BDS | Record used in an analysis | Filter on it when the SAP says so |
| `ASTDT`, `TRTEMFL` | OCCDS | Analysis start date; treatment-emergent flag | Window usually closes at `TRTEDT` plus a lag; partial dates need a rule |

: The ADaM variable card. {#tbl-adam-card}

## Further reading

- CDISC Foundational Standards at
  `cdisc.org/standards/foundational`, the authoritative reference
  for SDTM and ADaM.
- [@mancini2026admiral], the `admiral` package and its vignettes,
  which derive every common ADaM dataset in R.
- [@fda2024conformance], the FDA Study Data Technical Conformance
  Guide, which states what a submission must contain.
- [@ich2025e6r3], the ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice guideline,
  for its risk-based approach to computerized systems and data
  governance.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-19}

1. SDTM (Study Data Tabulation Model) holds the submitted record
   of the collected clinical data, organized into domains such as
   `DM`, `AE`, `LB`, and `EX`. ADaM (Analysis Data Model) holds
   analysis-ready datasets derived from SDTM. In industry,
   statistical programmers typically build ADaM against
   specifications written or reviewed by the biostatistician, who
   also writes the SAP; SDTM is built by data management or
   clinical programmers.
2. A censored observation. `CNSR = 0` is the event, and other
   positive integers may code other censoring reasons; pass
   `CNSR == 0` to `survival::Surv()` as the event.
3. `ADSL` is the subject-level anchor dataset, with exactly one
   row per subject: treatment assignment, demographics, baseline
   covariates, key dates, and population flags. Every other ADaM
   dataset (`ADLB`, `ADTTE`, `ADAE`) joins back to `ADSL` by
   `USUBJID` and takes treatment and population flags from it.
